prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms held at a magic wavelength enable frequency measurement with accuracy and stability at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B004, for Katori and Ye. After reading all eight first-round statements, the case seems to me to rest on three things an experimentalist can check. First, the invention is specific: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap-induced shift while keeping thousands of atoms interrogated at once, which is what separates it from a single trapped ion. Second, the realisation is demonstrable: Ye's group took it to the 1e-18 regime and used the ensemble to resolve many-body and gravitational-redshift effects at sub-millimetre scales, which a single-ion clock cannot do. Third, the result has been reproduced and compared across laboratories for about two decades, so the claim does not depend on one group's word. Seven of eight members reach the same two names, but I do not count that as evidence. The scientific case is what persuades me, and it would persuade me with fewer supporters.
statement.case_against: The distinctness question the chair asks remains the real reservation, and I do not think it can be dismissed. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems, and both are ingredients of every optical clock. My answer is that the lattice clock changes what is measured: an ensemble rather than a single ion, with a systematic that is removed by design rather than tolerated. That is an argument I find convincing, but I accept it is a judgement and that Danielsson, Kroll and Pearce are right that it is a metrology step more than a new phenomenon in nature. Credit also remains imperfect: Takamoto and colleagues in Katori's group, and the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups, fall outside two names, and I cannot verify the priority record from what has been supplied. I regard the redefinition of the second as supporting evidence only, not a condition: the clock's performance has been demonstrated whether or not the metrology bodies act.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B004 but says a prize for an instrument and measurement capability weighs less than a clue found in nature, and fears the committee is choosing the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery (B032).
responses.response: I take that fear seriously, and the allocation problem is the reason I do not follow you to B032. A three-name IceCube prize would exclude people whose roles none of us can verify from the record, whereas I can state the lattice clock's credit with two names. Where I do not agree is that the clock is only an instrument. Its significance lies in what it measures: gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample and constraints on drifting constants and dark-sector couplings, which are observations about nature. I would still say that if IceCube's source associations sharpen further, it deserves a fresh hearing in a later year, and I would not want that to be read as a ruling against it now.

responses.point: Kroll says the credited pair omits Takamoto and others in Katori's group, and that the redefinition of the second is a prospective payoff that does not alter the science. He also discloses a doctoral research stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA, Ye's institution.
responses.response: On the redefinition, I agree with you and answer the chair's question the same way: it is supporting evidence, not a condition. On credit, I think we should be honest that a prize rewards a named idea and its decisive realisation, and that Takamoto's first Sr lattice measurements were made in Katori's own group, which is part of what the proposal-plus-realisation split captures. I have no concern about your Boulder stay: a doctoral period in a laboratory that is not Ye's own group, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a disclosure and nothing more. I would not ask you to step back from B004 deliberations.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B010 as a single part for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, keeps B004 as first alternative, and argues that the 2011 prediction is a joint result so dropping Bistritzer would create a hard-to-defend attribution problem. He accepts that the field is about eight years old and that the pairing mechanism is debated.
responses.response: You have persuaded me on Bistritzer: the 2011 paper is joint and I was wrong to treat the third name as a spare seat. That changes my view of B010's attribution, but not of its timing. I ranked it first in my opening, so I am not setting it aside lightly, and I think your case is the strongest alternative on the list. My reservation is that the three names would still sit beside the unresolved first-author contribution of the 2018 papers, and I would want to see the pairing mechanism settle before we fix the credit. If B004 is not carried, I would support B010 next, and I would be glad to see it return in a later cycle.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, supports B004 but names the overlap with the comb and cavity-stabilised-laser technology of earlier prizes as the strongest reservation, saying that Ye's record rests partly on already recognised technology.
responses.response: I agree that Ye's record builds on comb and cavity-stabilised-laser technology, and I think that should be said openly in the citation process rather than hidden. But the earlier prizes honoured those tools; they did not honour using an ensemble of neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice to reach 1e-18 stability. That is why my citation names the lattice and the magic wavelength explicitly and does not mention timekeeping in general, so that the new step is what is credited. I would not accept a citation that reads as a general prize for optical clocks.

uncertainties: Whether the distinctness of the lattice clock from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a scientific fact or a committee judgement; I believe the former but cannot prove it.
Whether the supplied record fully captures priority between Katori's group, including Takamoto, and other Sr and Yb groups; I cannot verify the early history.
Whether magic-angle graphene is premature only because of the pairing mechanism, or also because experimental credit is still being reordered; I have not verified the early experimental history.
Johansson's reference to Ye under other candidate lines: the shortlist shows Ye only under B004, so I treat it as an error unless Johansson says otherwise.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B004, B010 or B009. I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Moodera, Miyazaki or Parkin. My Japanese academic exchanges and microscopy leadership are general and do not bear on the optical-clock candidates. My shared Chalmers affiliation with Göran Johansson, whose opening first choice was B034, does not bear on my configuration. After reading Kroll's disclosure, I see no need for any step beyond disclosure.
